title: Wolters Kluwer’s Suzanne Konstance on Trust, Compliance, and the Next Phase of Legal AI
author: Suzanne Konstance

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Konstance accepts the cluster’s core view that legal AI has bounded, use-case-specific value and requires expert verification and redesigned human roles. She materially develops it by identifying authoritative, current and structured content, editorial review, customer co-design, and users’ capacity to audit and challenge agentic systems as concrete prerequisites for trustworthy deployment.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Konstance supports the cluster’s core proposition that adaptation requires continuous, selective learning and human judgment rather than passive technology adoption. She emphasizes developing the ability to understand, audit and challenge AI, while describing professional exchanges and industry channels as sources of ongoing awareness. Wolters Kluwer’s dedicated AI practice also illustrates organisational support for this learning, though the source does not assess channel effectiveness or provide measured outcomes.

kp.k: Customers prioritise research accuracy over speed and efficiency
kp.d: Konstance reports that customers asked about AI return on investment, speed and efficiency instead emphasise quality and accuracy, especially for legal research rather than uses such as summarisation, emails and checklists. This is vendor-reported customer feedback, without a stated sample size or quantified results.
qs: And we’ll ask things about like return on investment and speed and efficiency. And usually they’ll come back and they’ll say, quality, accuracy. That’s what I’m focused on right now.
but with the research and actually getting to the right content, they’ll often say, I’m really focused on accuracy at this point.

kp.k: Trustworthy AI requires authoritative, current, contextualised content
kp.d: Konstance argues that content value extends beyond a document's text to its authority, regulatory history, subsequent actions, context and metadata. These features help search and AI tools find and use information appropriately; sophisticated research tools cannot compensate for inaccurate, limited or outdated inputs.
qs: Where we focus is on making sure when we’re providing content that we know where the content is coming from.
Has it changed over time? Has there been action against it? Are there updates? Are there arguments that affect it?
also mentioned meta tagging and making sure that you categorize information so that all these tools can actually use it correctly
So AI, the best, sophisticated, deep research tool that you can get based on inaccurate information, limited information, out of date information is going to get you in a bad spot.

kp.k: Regulatory change increases the importance of editorial expertise
kp.d: Konstance positions Wolters Kluwer's regulatory work around helping customers remain compliant and avoid litigation, including securities, tax, IP and employment. She says rapid regulatory changes and executive orders increase the importance of authors and editors who update content and explain its implications. She describes multiple levels of editorial review, whether regulation is increasing, changing or being reduced.
qs: our focus is helping our customers stay out of litigation.
we’re constantly providing updates on changes to regulation as well as things like executive orders.
those authors and those editors are even more critical right now with all the change that we have
we have a whole process of review and levels of editorial review.

kp.k: Harvey licensing extends content into external AI workflows
kp.d: Host Greg Lambert describes a recently formalised non-exclusive licence giving Harvey access to primary-source legal content from the US and German divisions. Konstance explains that the country businesses made their respective decisions and that the US objective was better accuracy and outcomes for Harvey users, alongside learning how Wolters Kluwer content is used in the evolving ecosystem. These are strategic objectives, not measured improvements; she specifies that the licensed primary material is only a subset of its content.
qs: granting them what’s called a non-exclusive access to primary source legal content from both its US and its German divisions.
I made this decision for the Legal and Regulatory US
what we saw was we had an opportunity to really add better accuracy, better results for those customers using Harvey.
And for us, it’s a way to see also how our information is used and how it applies in this ecosystem.
And the data we provided was primary. So it’s really a subset of the data and the content that we have

kp.k: Internal AI development complements selective ecosystem partnerships
kp.d: Konstance describes parallel investment in AI within Wolters Kluwer's own products and collaboration with external AI providers. Internal development targets specific practice areas and use cases through experiments with clients, particularly superusers. External content provision is conditional on suitable use cases, content the business is comfortable releasing, and partners sharing its accuracy objectives; Harvey is one collaborator rather than the entire strategy.
qs: Harvey is one collaborator
we have a significant investment and focus on building out AI tools within our products.
we are partnering very closely with clients on that and doing experiments with, especially our super users in certain areas
when it makes sense, when it’s a use case that makes sense, we’ll provide the content
with partners that we feel have the same kind of objective to do to provide the right accurate information for clients

kp.k: Editors and customer feedback support ongoing product refinement
kp.d: Konstance says the Vital Law AI product incorporates editors who curate answers and subject-specific information around commonly asked questions. Feedback from existing customers, not just development participants, is used to refine the product. She acknowledges that even increasingly sophisticated tools are imperfect and stresses transparency about what the tool uses and the technology's evolving limitations.
qs: So incorporated in our Vital Law AI product, have editors in the loop.
So they’re very much involved in curating the information and providing as much good content as possible at a different level
They’re constantly giving us feedback which we can turn around to continue to refine the solution.
It isn’t ever perfect, so it’s very important that there is transparency
sometimes the sizzle in the market can get a little bit much.

kp.k: Hands-on testing highlights demand for citation transparency
kp.d: Konstance recounts sandbox sessions at AALL where users were invited to challenge the tools rather than watch guided demonstrations. She reports average participation of about 30 minutes and an enthusiastic response to seeing citations and source information as the tool worked. She says participants requested expanded capabilities, including cross-jurisdictional work. This is a vendor account of user testing, not a formal accuracy benchmark; her statement that nobody broke the tool does not establish an error rate.

kp.k: Legal AI product adoption involves multiple professional groups
kp.d: Konstance describes law librarians as important intermediaries selecting tools and content for large firms, while attorneys are the ultimate users needing reliable information. Highly engaged practice specialists contribute detailed feedback. The customer and user base also includes corporate legal departments, academics and students, government entities and sometimes compliance professionals.
qs: we often will work with law librarians when we’re working with large law firms, because they’re trying to bring in the right tools, the right content for their base.
There’s, course, attorneys are our ultimate customer.
We also have academics who are learning and
working with their students on the use of the content, the information, but also the technology and government entities as well.
Sometimes compliance professionals also get involved with our solutions.

kp.k: Human verification remains necessary despite persuasive AI outputs
kp.d: Konstance argues that models can struggle when supplied information has gaps or imbalances and can produce persuasive responses disconnected from reality. Using a personal travel-planning example rather than legal performance data, she recommends retaining control, editing and independently cross-checking outputs rather than delegating reliance to the system.
qs: If there’s gaps in what you’re feeding it or if there’s too much of a certain thing
It’ll tell you what you want to hear. And sometimes it is really not based on reality.
You can’t give up the reins of control.
like you have to be on top of this and realize that you’re still editing this.
Like I should have in that instant done some of my own cross-checking

kp.k: Agentic research shifts professionals toward supervisory work
kp.d: In the future-oriented discussion, Konstance predicts a shift from passive search toward deploying and managing active AI agents. She compares this responsibility to supervising 30 high-school interns with differing abilities: specifying desired outcomes, providing detailed instructions, ensuring productivity and preventing trouble. Her suggestion that there are probably fewer individual contributors is a qualitative role-change claim, not workforce evidence or a quantified employment forecast.
qs: there are probably way less individual contributors anymore because we’re all managing agents and ⁓ these little helpers.
one summer I inherited or just was given 30 high school interns.
And I had to manage them and make sure that they were productive, make sure they didn’t get into any trouble.
it’s not this passive, I go in, I put my search in, I get information. We’re gonna be deploying agents.
It’s very polished and looks very comprehensive, but we are going to have to manage it very carefully.

kp.k: AI supervision raises expertise and newcomer training requirements
kp.d: Konstance argues that supervising AI requires understanding the steps of manual work and comparing AI work against them, making professional proficiency more rather than less important. She identifies bringing newcomers up to speed quickly as a future challenge and recommends teaching fundamentals together with the ability to criticise, audit and challenge technology. No specific training programme or measured learning outcome is supplied.
qs: we have to get back to the basics of understanding the steps that we would have taken in a completely manual environment
So folks have to be even more proficient at what they do.
how do we bring new folks in the industry up as quickly as possible?
we’re going to have to work with people to understand the basics and to criticize, audit, challenge, you know, some of the technology so that they can manage the AI and not be managed.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Konstance says legal-research AI's usefulness depends on authoritative, current, contextualised content; customers currently prioritise accuracy over speed or return on investment.
pts.d: Suzanne Konstance, speaking as vice president and general manager of Wolters Kluwer Legal and Regulatory US, reports that customers distinguish research from uses such as summarisation, emails and checklists. For research, they emphasise finding the correct information. She argues that sophisticated AI cannot compensate for inaccurate, incomplete or outdated sources. Provenance, regulatory history, context and metadata remain important to retrieving and using information correctly.

pts.k: Konstance presents content licensing and embedded AI tools as complementary ways to improve legal workflows.
pts.d: She describes the Harvey AI collaboration as an opportunity to improve accuracy and outcomes by supplying trusted information, not as a demonstrated performance improvement. The supplied material is primary content and only a subset of Wolters Kluwer's holdings. In parallel, she describes investment in proprietary AI tools, practice-specific use cases and customer experiments. Wolters Kluwer and Harvey are discussed here as content/software providers, not as alternative legal service providers delivering legal work.

pts.k: Konstance says editorial involvement, customer feedback and transparency are necessary as legal AI evolves, but do not make it perfect.
pts.d: She describes editors curating subject-specific content and answers for Vital Law AI, with customer feedback used to refine the product. She argues that users need visibility into the information the tool uses, including citations. Her account of sandbox sessions illustrates demand for transparency and opportunities for product development, rather than establishing measured accuracy or freedom from hallucinations.

pts.k: Konstance predicts a shift from passive research and individual contribution toward supervising AI agents, requiring greater expertise and new approaches to training entrants.
pts.d: She frames legal-research AI as augmentation under continuing human control, not autonomous substitution on which users should rely unchecked. She predicts that people will increasingly specify tasks, supervise agents and verify polished outputs against the steps of manual work. Her statement about fewer individual contributors concerns changing roles; she does not quantify job losses or predict a particular law-firm staffing structure. She identifies rapid development of foundational expertise among new entrants as a challenge.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists mainly of customer conversations, internal product-development experience and anecdotal user testing.
pts.d: For customer priorities and product refinement, Konstance draws on regular client feedback and experiments with highly engaged users. For transparency, she recounts an AALL conference sandbox session, reporting approximately 30 minutes of average participation and an enthusiastic user's reaction. No participant count, accuracy benchmark, controlled comparison, measured hallucination rate or quantified return on investment is supplied. The Harvey benefits are stated objectives and opportunities, not reported evaluation results.

pts.k: The oversight argument and agent-management prediction are supported by personal experience and analogy, not labour-market evidence.
pts.d: Konstance uses a personal ChatGPT hotel-search experience to illustrate the consequences of inadequate source coverage and failing to cross-check an answer. She compares managing AI agents to an earlier experience managing 30 high-school interns with differing capabilities. These support her explanation of supervision requirements; neither is a legal-task benchmark or evidence of actual employment displacement.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account combines present-day observations in 2025 with an undated forecast of agent-based legal research; benefits remain conditional on source quality, appropriate partnerships and human oversight.
pts.d: Customer emphasis on accuracy and the editorial-feedback processes are described as current. Konstance says additional cross-border AI tools will be released in several days, but provides no adoption or impact timetable. Her role-change forecast mixes changes already underway with future deployment of agents and gives no year or quantitative forecast. Further content provision is conditional on suitable use cases, acceptable content and aligned partners. She explicitly cautions that capabilities are evolving and users cannot relinquish control.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are legal researchers and practitioners, librarians, corporate legal departments, compliance professionals, educators, new entrants and legal-information providers.
pts.d: Attorneys are the ultimate users expected to obtain reliable information and supervise AI-assisted work. Law librarians in large firms help select tools and content and participate in testing. Corporate legal departments, government entities, academics and sometimes compliance professionals also use the products. New entrants face the challenge of learning enough substantive and procedural expertise to challenge AI outputs. Editors and subject-matter experts contribute curated information and product refinement; providers pursue both internal AI development and collaborations. The interview does not offer a distinct prediction about consumer access to justice, legal fees or law-firm headcount.
